title: AWS access management: IAM, root user, Identity Center and credentials
learningObjective: Explain IAM users, groups, roles and policies, least privilege, root user protection and root-only tasks, IAM Identity Center and federation, MFA, access keys, password policies and credential storage.
foundation: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls who can sign in (authentication) and what they can do (authorization) in your AWS account.
The root user is the email account that created the AWS account. It has full power, so protect it with MFA and use it only for the few tasks that require it.
Give people only the permissions they need (least privilege), preferably through groups and roles, and sign in through IAM Identity Center.
engineer: IAM entities: users (long-term credentials; minimise), groups (collections of users; attach policies), roles (temporary credentials assumed by users, services or other accounts), policies (JSON: Effect, Action, Resource, Condition). AWS managed policies vs customer managed policies vs inline policies.

Evaluation: explicit Deny wins; otherwise an explicit Allow is needed; everything else is implicitly denied. SCPs in AWS Organizations set the maximum permissions for member accounts (including their root user).

Root user: enable MFA, do not create root access keys, use for root-only tasks such as changing account settings (name, email, root password), closing the account, restoring IAM permissions when locked out, configuring S3 MFA delete, and registering as a seller in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

Authentication: passwords with an IAM password policy, MFA (virtual authenticator, FIDO security keys, hardware TOTP), access keys for programmatic access (rotate, avoid on root), temporary credentials via roles (STS).

IAM Identity Center: central workforce access to multiple accounts and apps with permission sets, using its own directory or an external identity provider (federation with SAML/OIDC, for example Microsoft Entra ID or Okta). Cross-account roles grant access between accounts.
Credential storage: AWS Secrets Manager (secrets with automatic rotation) and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (configuration and SecureString parameters).

example.title: Hardening a new account
body: The founder enables MFA on the root user and stores its credentials securely. Staff sign in through IAM Identity Center federated with the company's identity provider, receiving permission sets such as ReadOnlyAccess or a custom least-privilege set. Apps on EC2 use IAM roles and read database passwords from Secrets Manager.

prerequisites: An AWS account (use an IAM Identity Center user, not root)
permissions: Read-only access to explore; least-privilege permissions to change resources
limits: Conceptual objective: explore in the console; no configuration limits are tested
portal: Secrets Manager > Store a new secret.
configuration.cli:
aws iam get-account-summary
aws iam update-account-password-policy --minimum-password-length 14 --require-symbols
aws iam create-group --group-name Developers && aws iam attach-group-policy --group-name Developers --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name prod/db --secret-string '{"password":"..."}'
configuration.powershell:
Get-IAMAccountSummary
New-IAMGroup -GroupName Developers
Register-IAMGroupPolicy -GroupName Developers -PolicyArn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess

lab.objective: Predict IAM decisions and identify root-only tasks.
steps: IAM policy evaluation: apply each preset.
Root user tasks: answer every task.
expected: Explicit deny wins; SCP limits even root
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.cause: An explicit Deny or SCP applies.
troubleshooting.fix: Check SCPs and all attached policies.

troubleshooting.symptom: Leaked access keys in a public repo.
troubleshooting.fix: Deactivate and rotate keys; prefer roles and temporary credentials.

comparisons.difference: Azure separates directory (Entra ID) from resource authorization (RBAC); AWS IAM covers both within an account.

misconceptions.myth: The root user should be used for administration.
misconceptions.reality: Use IAM Identity Center or IAM roles; root only for root tasks.

architectureDecisions: Federate workforce access through IAM Identity Center; use roles for workloads; enforce MFA.

walkthrough.subtitle: Fix a startup where everyone shares the root password, one step at a time.
learn: Protect the root user and know the root-only tasks
IAM users, groups, roles and policies
Least privilege with managed and custom policies
Credentials: MFA, access keys, password policy, Secrets Manager

steps.label: Shared root
steps.title: Everyone signs in as root
body: A startup's five engineers all use the root user: the email and password that created the AWS account. Root can do everything, including closing the account.
One leaked password could lose the whole company.

steps.label: Lock root
steps.title: Lock away the root user
body: Turn on MFA for root, don't create root access keys, and store the credentials safely. Use root only for the few tasks that need it.

Root-only tasks include changing the account name, email or root password, closing the account, restoring IAM permissions when you are locked out, configuring S3 MFA Delete, and registering as a seller in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

callout.text: Protect root with MFA and don't use it for daily work.

steps.label: Groups + policies
steps.title: Give people their own identities
body: Each engineer gets their own identity. Put users with the same job in an IAM group and attach a policy to the group. A policy is a JSON document that allows or denies actions on resources.
When someone changes job, move them to another group.

steps.label: Least privilege
steps.title: Grant only what's needed
body: Least privilege means each identity gets only the permissions its task needs, nothing more. Start with AWS managed policies, which AWS writes and maintains. Write customer managed policies when you need something narrower.
In IAM an explicit Deny always wins, and anything not allowed is denied.

callout.text: AWS managed policies are convenient but often broad. Custom policies let you be exact.

steps.label: Identity Center
steps.title: One sign-in for every account
body: IAM Identity Center gives your workforce a single sign-in to all your AWS accounts and business apps. Identities can live in Identity Center itself or in your existing company directory. Using an existing directory is called federation.
People use their normal work login, and leavers lose access in one place.

steps.label: Roles
steps.title: Use roles for temporary access
body: An IAM role has permissions but no password. A user, an AWS service such as EC2, or another account assumes the role and gets temporary credentials.
Cross-account roles let your auditors' account read your logs without sharing any keys.

steps.label: Credentials
steps.title: Handle credentials safely
body: Set a password policy (length, complexity) and require MFA. Access keys are for programs, not people: rotate them and never put them in code.
Store database passwords and API keys in AWS Secrets Manager, which can rotate them automatically, or in Systems Manager Parameter Store.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: From one shared password to proper access
body: Each person and program now has the access it needs, and no more.
recap: Root: MFA, no access keys, only root-only tasks
Users in groups; policies attached to groups; roles for temporary access
Identity Center + federation for workforce sign-in
MFA, password policy, rotated keys, Secrets Manager
